architectural_implications.after: Four tools spanning chunks, sections, full documents and corpus enumeration, with the agent choosing escalation.
architectural_implications.before: A single retrieve(query, k) function feeding a fixed context window.
architectural_implications.consequence: Retrieval policy moves from code into the agent loop, increasing latency and nondeterminism but enabling multi-hop resolution of cross-references.
architectural_implications.observation: Retrieval granularity is exposed as multiple callable tools rather than one top-k endpoint.

architectural_implications.after: UI renders streamed markdown incrementally and appends validated source cards when the object finalizes.
architectural_implications.before: App expects a single JSON/Pydantic response rendered on completion.
architectural_implications.consequence: Client must handle an intermediate state with prose but no citations; the schema contract becomes an event sequence, not a single payload.
architectural_implications.observation: Structured and unstructured outputs travel on different channels.

architectural_implications.after: Regex/section-aware text chunks (≤2,000 chars) plus a dedicated CSV-serialized table path, both embedded densely and BM25.
architectural_implications.before: One chunker over extracted PDF text.
architectural_implications.consequence: Indexing complexity rises but retrieval correctness for numeric/relational content stops depending on chunk boundary luck.
architectural_implications.observation: Table and text ingestion are separate pipelines in the offline index.

article_ideas.angle: Show the concrete failure mode — a fee type spanning multiple rows getting mapped to the wrong columns — then argue that the fix is pipeline topology (dual ingestion paths, CSV row serialization) and that no amount of retrieval tuning recovers from corrupted chunk content.
article_ideas.audience: RAG/retrieval engineers and data platform teams ingesting PDFs with financial, compliance or spec tables
article_ideas.thesis: In document RAG, table handling is an architectural boundary rather than a preprocessing detail: any pipeline that lets a character-window chunker touch a structured region produces fluent, well-cited, wrong numeric answers, so the retrieval index must carry region-type-specific extraction paths with a hard rule that a table is never split.
article_ideas.title: Your Chunker Is Lying About Your Tables

article_ideas.angle: Push back on the universally-quoted 5-point number: argue for paired reporting (retrieval hit rate alongside answer accuracy on the same query set) and show why domains full of codes, identifiers and message names make dense-only retrieval structurally unfixable.
article_ideas.audience: AI engineers and evaluation leads shipping production RAG
article_ideas.based_on: Hybrid dense + BM25 retrieval combined via reciprocal rank fusion raised hit rate from 92% to 97%
article_ideas.thesis: Hybrid dense+BM25 fusion with reciprocal rank fusion gets cited as a 92%→97% win, but retrieval hit rate is a proxy that can move independently of end-to-end grounded-answer correctness and citation accuracy; hybrid search should be adopted as the baseline by default for symbolic corpora, and the remaining gap should be measured at the answer level before anyone claims a quality improvement.
article_ideas.title: Retrieval Hit Rate Is Not an Answer Metric

article_ideas.angle: Treat latency as a first-class product surface: frame the 38s median as a signal that agentic retrieval's cost scales with tool turns, and argue that progressive disclosure and a text-then-source-cards UI contract are the only defensible UX once you accept multi-turn retrieval.
article_ideas.audience: Product engineers and architects building agentic interfaces on top of retrieval systems
article_ideas.based_on: Median answer time of 38 seconds for a small research task.
article_ideas.thesis: Multi-step agentic retrieval turns a chat completion into a small research task, and the honest response is to redesign the product contract around that latency — streaming the reasoning and prose, attaching provenance at completion — instead of pretending the system is a chat reply and hiding dead air behind a spinner.
article_ideas.title: 38 Seconds Is a Design Decision, Not a Bug

article_ideas.angle: Reframe retrieval design as an API-surface question: four tools with different cost and granularity plus an explicit escalation policy, then confront the discipline problem the talk leaves open.
article_ideas.audience: Software architects and agent-platform engineers designing retrieval APIs
article_ideas.based_on: Agent chooses from four tools depending on query complexity
article_ideas.thesis: Exposing retrieval at multiple zoom levels — chunk search, section fetch, full-document fetch, corpus enumeration — as separate tools moves retrieval granularity from an index-time constant to a runtime decision, which is the only way cross-reference-heavy corpora get resolved without stuffing everything into the prompt; the cost is that retrieval policy leaves your code and enters a nondeterministic agent loop, so escalation must be budgeted.
article_ideas.title: Stop Building One retrieve(query, k) Endpoint

connections.concept: zoomable retrieval tools (chunks → sections → full document)
connections.relationship: Retrieval granularity becomes a runtime policy decision delegated to the agent loop instead of a fixed index-time parameter.

connections.concept: reciprocal rank fusion of dense + BM25
connections.relationship: Fusion repairs the class of misses dense embeddings structurally cannot cover (codes, identifiers, message names).
Preserving row-column relations is a precondition for correct numeric answers that are then attributed back to a page and section.
Schema validation and incremental rendering are in tension, resolved by separate text and source-card channels.

connections.concept: per-interaction logging to Azure Table Storage
connections.relationship: Captured interaction logs are the raw material for offline evaluation and judge-rubric calibration.

evidence_quotes.text: Never split tables across chunks.
Table rows formatted as CSV to preserve relational context across rows.
Tables must be parsed and converted into CSV text format to prevent cross-row field mapping errors.

core_insights.generalization: Any RAG over documents with dense structured regions (financial tables, spec matrices, compliance schedules) needs region-type-specific extraction paths and a rule that a structured region is never split across chunks.
core_insights.insight: Treating tables as a first-class, separately-parsed artifact (rows serialized as CSV text) rather than letting a generic page-level chunker ingest them prevents cross-row field misalignment in retrieved fee/rate data.
core_insights.why_it_matters: Generic character-window chunking silently corrupts tabular semantics: a fee type spanning multiple rows gets mapped to the wrong columns, producing plausible but wrong answers that are hard to catch downstream. A dedicated table pipeline is an architectural boundary, not a preprocessing nicety.

evidence_quotes.text: Combining dense and BM25 via reciprocal rank fusion improves hit rate from 92% to 97%.
Hit rate improved from 92% (dense only) to 97% (hybrid).

core_insights.generalization: For domains with symbolic vocabularies (codes, IDs, SKUs, error strings, legal citations), dense-only retrieval has a measurably irreducible miss rate; sparse+fusion should be the baseline and dense-only must be justified.
core_insights.insight: Hybrid dense + BM25 retrieval combined via reciprocal rank fusion raised hit rate from 92% to 97% over dense-only in a corpus dominated by exact codes, identifiers and message names.
core_insights.why_it_matters: It quantifies a concrete 5-point gap and attributes it to a specific failure mode of dense retrieval — exact token lookups (device type codes, message names). That makes the hybrid decision an evidence-backed default rather than a preference.

evidence_quotes.text: Agent chooses from four tools depending on query complexity: search rulebooks, retrieve rulebook sections, retrieve full rulebook, or list available rulebooks.
Agentic retrieval with tool discipline beats single-shot RAG.
Agent uses search_rulebooks first, then retrieve_rulebook_sections if needed.

core_insights.generalization: Expose your retrieval index at multiple zoom levels as separate tools with explicit escalation policy; let the agent pay for more context only on demand. This is a zoomable-retrieval abstraction that generalizes to code search, legal, and internal docs.
core_insights.insight: Retrieval is exposed to the model as four distinct tools with different cost/granularity (search chunks, fetch sections, fetch a full rulebook, enumerate available rulebooks), and the agent is expected to sequence them (search first, then escalate to section retrieval).
core_insights.why_it_matters: This reframes retrieval granularity as a runtime decision rather than an index-time constant. The agent can escalate context size only when the cheaper search is insufficient, which is how cross-reference-heavy corpora (~2,000 cross-references) get resolved without stuffing everything into the prompt.

evidence_quotes.text: You cannot stream partial Pydantic objects; answers must be split into streamed markdown text followed by attached source cards.
Stream markdown text token-by-token and attach source cards afterward.

core_insights.generalization: When output schemas must be validated, split the response into a streamable unstructured channel and a terminal structured channel; design the client to render partial text and reconcile structured attachments on completion.
core_insights.insight: Streaming structured output is impossible at the object level: a Pydantic response object cannot be partially streamed, so the answer is decomposed into token-streamed markdown text plus source cards attached at the end.
core_insights.why_it_matters: It is a concrete constraint of typed/schema-validated outputs versus perceived latency, and it dictates a UI contract: the schema-bearing part (citations, provenance) arrives after the natural-language part. Ignoring this produces either unvalidated JSON streaming or a long dead-air wait.

evidence_quotes.text: Enrich chunks with metadata like document name, page numbers, section hierarchy, and LLM-generated summaries.
Keep document structure and section paths as metadata.

core_insights.generalization: Index both the raw content and a machine-generated synopsis per chunk, and carry the document's structural path as filterable metadata — this is what enables zoom-level retrieval and verifiable citation.
core_insights.insight: Chunk metadata is enriched with structural path information — document name, page numbers, section hierarchy — plus LLM-generated per-chunk summaries, so citations and section-aware retrieval are derived from indexing-time structure rather than reconstructed at query time.
core_insights.why_it_matters: Section hierarchy as metadata is what makes the 'retrieve sections' tool and grounded citations possible; the LLM-generated summary field adds a retrieval surface that isn't a verbatim substring of the page.

evidence_quotes.text: Median answer time of 38 seconds for a small research task.
A median of 38 seconds per answer. It is not just a chat reply, it is a small research task.

core_insights.generalization: Agentic retrieval latency scales roughly with number of tool turns; plan for tens of seconds and design progressive disclosure (streamed reasoning/text) instead of pretending it's a chat completion.
core_insights.insight: Published latency for this agentic retrieval loop is a median of ~38 seconds per answer, which the speakers explicitly reframe as a research task rather than a chat reply.
core_insights.why_it_matters: Multi-step tool-using retrieval has a latency profile an order of magnitude worse than single-shot RAG; that number should drive product framing, streaming strategy and UX expectations, and it makes latency a first-class optimization target.

evidence_quotes.text: Median answer time of 38 seconds for a small research task.
A median of 38 seconds per answer. It is not just a chat reply, it is a small research task.

deep_dives.research_question: Where does the 38-second median answer time actually go — planner/model turns, number of tool calls, vector-DB query time, or context-size-driven generation cost — and what fraction is recoverable without losing answer quality?
deep_dives.topic: Latency decomposition of agentic multi-step retrieval
deep_dives.trigger_insight: Median answer time of 38 seconds for a small research task.
deep_dives.why: If most of the 38s is per-turn model latency multiplied by tool turns, the optimization lever is escalation policy, not the vector DB. Without a per-stage breakdown, teams will optimize the wrong component and mis-set UX expectations for research-style answers.

evidence_quotes.text: Agent chooses from four tools depending on query complexity: search rulebooks, retrieve rulebook sections, retrieve full rulebook, or list available rulebooks.
Agent uses search_rulebooks first, then retrieve_rulebook_sections if needed.
Agentic retrieval with tool discipline beats single-shot RAG.

deep_dives.research_question: Does a hard tool-call budget or cost-weighted tool selection beat prompt-level 'tool discipline' instructions on quality-per-second when an agent has search-chunks, fetch-section, fetch-full-document and list-corpus tools available?
deep_dives.topic: Escalation policy and tool-call budgets for zoomable retrieval
deep_dives.trigger_insight: Agentic retrieval with tool discipline beats single-shot RAG.
deep_dives.why: 'Tool discipline' is asserted as the thing that makes agentic retrieval beat single-shot RAG, but no policy mechanism is described. Escalation to full-rulebook retrieval is the most expensive and least precise action, so making that decision a guarded runtime policy rather than a prompt hope is the difference between a 38s research task and an unbounded one.

evidence_quotes.text: Combining dense and BM25 via reciprocal rank fusion improves hit rate from 92% to 97%.
Hit rate improved from 92% (dense only) to 97% (hybrid).

deep_dives.research_question: Does the 92%→97% reciprocal-rank-fusion hit-rate gain survive translation into final answer correctness and citation accuracy, or does the ~5-point retrieval gain collapse at the answer level?
deep_dives.topic: Retrieval hit rate versus end-to-end grounded-answer accuracy
deep_dives.why: A retrieval metric that does not predict answer quality will cause teams to ship hybrid search and then misattribute remaining errors to the model. The reporting gap is the cheapest place to catch this: pair the retrieval numbers with end-to-end grounded-answer accuracy on the same query set.

evidence_quotes.text: Enrich chunks with metadata like document name, page numbers, section hierarchy, and LLM-generated summaries.
Table rows formatted as CSV to preserve relational context across rows.

deep_dives.research_question: Which enrichment actually buys retrieval and answer accuracy: whole-table CSV serialization, section-hierarchy metadata, LLM-generated per-chunk summaries, or the section-aware chunk boundary itself?
deep_dives.topic: Ablating chunk-enrichment mechanisms (CSV tables vs section path vs LLM summaries)
deep_dives.trigger_insight: Enrich chunks with metadata like document name, page numbers, section hierarchy, and LLM-generated summaries.
deep_dives.why: All four are bundled as one 'good ingestion' story, so a team adopting the approach cannot tell which expensive step to keep. LLM-generated summaries in particular add a full generation pass over every chunk; if the gain is concentrated in table handling and section paths, the summary pass is pure cost.

evidence_quotes.text: You cannot stream partial Pydantic objects; answers must be split into streamed markdown text followed by attached source cards.
Stream markdown text token-by-token and attach source cards afterward.

deep_dives.research_question: Can incremental/partial JSON parsing with progressive schema validation restore perceived responsiveness for typed responses, or is the two-channel split (streamed prose, terminal structured payload) forced?
deep_dives.topic: Streaming contracts for schema-validated agent output
deep_dives.trigger_insight: You cannot stream partial Pydantic objects
deep_dives.why: The claim treats non-streamable Pydantic objects as a hard constraint, which turns into a permanent product experience: users read prose with no provenance until the very end. If partial validation works, the citation UI can render progressively and the two-channel contract becomes an implementation choice rather than an architecture.

summary.html:
Overview

  • Speaker: Nina Žižakić & Eleonora Drykina
  • Channel: AI Engineer
  • Main topic: Unremarkable RAG in Production for Financial Rulebooks
  • Purpose: Explain technical decisions, architecture, and production lessons in building a RAG system for a financial institution dealing with 270 rulebooks, 6,000 PDF pages, and 3,000 tables. Nina Žižakić and Eleonora Drykina share real-world production insights on building a Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) system for a major Belgian financial institution's payment rulebooks. They walk through technical decisions including indexing, table processing as CSV, hybrid dense and BM25 search with reciprocal rank fusion, agentic retrieval with multiple tools, streaming responses with Pydantic object handling, and evaluation strategies.

Topic Map

Introduction and Problem Scale

  • Explanation: Introduction of speakers from In The Pocket and overview of the rulebooks dataset containing ~270 rulebooks, ~6,000 pages of PDF, ~3,000 tables, and ~2,000 cross-references.
  • Key claims:
    • Rulebooks contain unexpected nuggets like refrigerators being valid payment devices under device type definitions.
  • Examples:
    • Device type 3331 explicitly lists refrigerators and washing machines.
  • Terminology:
    • RAG
    • rulebooks
    • payment scheme
  • Why it matters: Establishes the domain complexity and scale of unstructured financial data.

Offline Indexing Pipeline

  • Explanation: The offline indexing pipeline splits PDF pages into chunks up to 2,000 characters, extracts section-aware chunks using regex, processes tables separately, and generates dense and BM25 embeddings.
  • Key claims:
    • Never split tables across chunks.
    • Enrich chunks with metadata like document name, page numbers, section hierarchy, and LLM-generated summaries.
  • Examples:
    • Table rows formatted as CSV to preserve relational context across rows.
  • Terminology:
    • dense embeddings
    • BM25
    • metadata enrichment
    • table processing
  • Why it matters: Good retrieval starts with proper document parsing, chunking, and metadata structuring.

Online Serving and Agentic Retrieval

  • Explanation: The online serving pipeline uses FastAPI, a vector database, and an agent using Google ADK with four retrieval tools to answer user queries with strict grounding and citations.
  • Key claims:
    • Agentic retrieval with tool discipline beats single-shot RAG.
    • Combining dense and BM25 via reciprocal rank fusion improves hit rate from 92% to 97%.
  • Examples:
    • Agent uses search_rulebooks first, then retrieve_rulebook_sections if needed.
  • Terminology:
    • agentic retrieval
    • reciprocal rank fusion
    • tool discipline
    • FastAPI
  • Why it matters: Financial RAG requires high precision, citations, and multi-step retrieval.

UI Streaming and Logging

  • Explanation: Handling Pydantic object streaming in UI and logging every user interaction into Azure Table Storage.
  • Key claims:
    • You cannot stream partial Pydantic objects; answers must be split into streamed markdown text followed by attached source cards.
  • Examples:
    • Median answer time of 38 seconds for a small research task.
  • Terminology:
    • Pydantic
    • streaming markdown
    • Azure Table Storage
  • Why it matters: Improves user experience during long retrieval and generation tasks.

Key Points

Table Special Processing

  • Explanation: Tables must be parsed and converted into CSV text format to prevent cross-row field mapping errors.
  • Evidence: Dummy example showing fee types spanning multiple rows parsed incorrectly without CSV conversion.
  • Practical implication: Significantly improves accuracy of fee and financial data retrieval.

Hybrid Search with Reciprocal Rank Fusion

  • Explanation: Combining dense embeddings for semantic meaning with BM25 for exact token matching overcomes code and identifier lookup failures.
  • Evidence: Hit rate improved from 92% (dense only) to 97% (hybrid).
  • Practical implication: Essential for domain-specific rulebooks containing exact codes and message names.

Frameworks, Models & Processes

Agentic Retrieval Pipeline

  • How it works: Agent chooses from four tools depending on query complexity: search rulebooks, retrieve rulebook sections, retrieve full rulebook, or list available rulebooks.
  • Components:
    • search_rulebooks
    • retrive_rulebook_sections
    • retrieve_full_rulebook
    • list_available_rulebooks
  • When to use: When questions require multi-step reasoning or pointing across multiple rulebook references.

Examples & Case Studies

Refrigerator categorized as a valid payment device under device type 3331.

  • Illustrates: Unexpected rules found in dry financial rulebooks.
  • Lesson: RAG enables discovery of edge cases buried deep in documentation.

Actionable Takeaways

  • Immediate:
    • Keep document structure and section paths as metadata.
    • Process tables with dedicated CSV pipelines.
    • Test with real users early.
  • Strategic:
    • Adopt agentic retrieval instead of single-shot RAG.
    • Stream markdown text token-by-token and attach source cards afterward.
  • Questions to investigate:
    • How to optimize agent retrieval latency below 38 seconds?
    • How to better calibrate LLM judge rubrics to avoid evaluation noise?

Claims Worth Verifying

  • Hybrid retrieval with reciprocal rank fusion improves hit rate from 92% to 97%. (metric)

Notable Quotes

"Your fridge is a valid payment device" (at 0:05) "A median of 38 seconds per answer. It is not just a chat reply, it is a small research task." (at 25:37)

Compressed Summary

  • Built production RAG for a major Belgian payment scheme rulebook repository.
  • Implemented table processing into CSV format to preserve relational data.
  • Combined dense embeddings and BM25 with reciprocal rank fusion achieving 97% hit rate.
  • Deployed agentic retrieval with 4 tools and LLM evaluation with promptfoo.
  • Keywords: rag, agentic retrieval, hybrid search, financial tech, vector database
  • Core insight: Building production RAG for financial rulebooks requires specialized table processing, hybrid search, and agentic multi-step tool retrieval rather than single-shot prompts.

## Key Points
### Table Special Processing
- **Explanation**: Tables must be parsed and converted into CSV text format to prevent cross-row field mapping errors.
- **Evidence**: Dummy example showing fee types spanning multiple rows parsed incorrectly without CSV conversion.

### Hybrid Search with Reciprocal Rank Fusion
- **Explanation**: Combining dense embeddings for semantic meaning with BM25 for exact token matching overcomes code and identifier lookup failures.
- **Evidence**: Hit rate improved from 92% (dense only) to 97% (hybrid).
- **Practical implication**: Essential for domain-specific rulebooks containing exact codes and message names.
## Frameworks, Models & Processes
### Agentic Retrieval Pipeline
- **How it works**: Agent chooses from four tools depending on query complexity: search rulebooks, retrieve rulebook sections, retrieve full rulebook, or list available rulebooks.
